query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the Hf content in HfMoTaTiZr by partially substituting Hf with an increased proportion of the lighter element Ti will decrease the alloy’s overall density while preserving its high yield strength and work hardening behavior at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr alloy (density ≈10.21 g/cm³) with a single BCC solid solution exhibiting high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Adjust the composition by lowering the Hf atomic fraction (for example, to about 50% of its original value) and compensating with a greater proportion of Ti—e.g., designing a modified alloy with nominal composition Hf0.5MoTaTiZr.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing should be performed on the as‐cast alloy under quasi‐static compressive (or tensile) loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures around 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The single-phase BCC solid solution microstructure is to be maintained via composition control and processing. With less Hf, the average atomic mass decreases while the lattice distortion, primarily provided by the remaining Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr, remains sufficient for solid-solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Hf is one of the heaviest elements in the alloy. By reducing its proportion and increasing Ti—a lighter element that can still participate effectively in BCC solid-solution strengthening—the overall density is reduced. Provided the lattice distortion and dislocation interaction remain adequate, the mechanical strength at both room and elevated temperatures is expected to be preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit a lowered density (a directional decrease relative to 10.21 g/cm³, on the order of a 10–15% decrease) while maintaining similar yield strength, work hardening behavior, and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C compared to the original HfMoTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr with high strength and a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis specifically applies to as‐cast BCC-structured high-entropy alloys tested under quasi-static loading conditions at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C; the effects outside of these conditions (e.g., very high strain rates or extreme environmental conditions) are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the observed effects from papers where adjustments of high‐density elements (e.g., Hf and Ta) and additions of light elements (such as Al or increased Ti content) led to reduced density without catastrophic loss of mechanical properties (see PMC7514121, PMC10254787, and related studies). The new aspect is applying a similar compositional reduction specifically to Hf in the HfMoTaTiZr system to mimic the beneficial design seen in low‐density Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloys, while ensuring that solid solution strengthening and grain structure are maintained. Uncertainty remains regarding the optimum substitution level and the potential influence on microstructural coarsening, which requires experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as‐cast alloys: one with the original equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr composition and a second with a reduced Hf content (targeting a composition such as Hf0.5MoTaTiZr). Process both alloys under identical conditions to ensure similar microstructures. Conduct quasi‐static compressive (or tensile) tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C to measure yield strength, plasticity, and work hardening. Additionally, determine the density of each alloy.
measurements: Yield strength at room temperature and ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy (Hf0.5MoTaTiZr) does not achieve a significant reduction in density (e.g., less than a 10% decrease relative to 10.21 g/cm³) or if its yield strength and ductility at room temperature and at ~1000 °C are significantly lower (more than 10–15% reduction) than those of the baseline HfMoTaTiZr, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Based on the existing simulation results, this paper reduces the atomic content of Ta and Hf at the same time to investigate their effects on the mechanical properties of the HEA, the tensile stress–strain curve obtained from the simulation is shown in Figure 4d. On the other hand, to further verify the accuracy of the simulation results, as-cast HfxNbTaxTiZr HEA samples (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) were prepared and tested to compare with the simulation results. The tensile stress–strain curve obtained from the test is shown in Figure 4e. The tensile yield strengths of HEAs with different compositions were calculated based on the simulation curves and compared with the tensile strengths obtained by testing. The comparison results are shown in Figure 4f. It can be seen from the comparison results that the variation trend of the simulated values is in line with the actual test results. The variation trend of dislocation density shown in Figure 5 also provides evidence.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
